full_judgment:
2. Brief facts are that the respondent, as plaintiff, filed the above money suit claiming decree for Taka 14,19,656, equivalent to US$ 29,140 at then rate, on the averments that the said amount is due from the defendant No. 2 appellant on account of supply of lubricant to their vessel, MV Loyal Bird, at different ports and during the pendency of the above money suit the plaintiff, suppressing the filing of the above Money Suit No. 21 of 1993 in Bangladeshi which was pending, also filed Admiralty Suit No. 44 of 1994 in the Bombay High Court claiming from the defendant No.2 the same very dues as claimed in the above money suit and got the above MV Loyal Bird, a Bangladeshi vessel, arrested while she went to India in connection with her voyage and due to above arrest MV Loyal Bird remained detained in India from 22-7-94 to 31-12-94 and consequently the defendant No.2 sustained business and other loss amounting to Taka 4,15,27,204; in the above circumstances, the defendant No.2, along with their written statements filed in the above Money Suit No. 21 of 1993 also filed a counter-claim claiming the said amount of Taka 4,15,27,204 against the plaintiff; on furnishing bank guarantee for the amount equivalent to Taka 14,19,656 as claimed by the plaintiff, the defendant No. 2 released MV Loyal Bird from Bombay High Court but after the said vessel returned to Bangladesh after its release, the plaintiff again, by suppressing facts, filed Admiralty Suit No. 20 of 1996 before the High Court Division and got the vessel arrested again for the same very claim and thus the plaintiff, for the same cause of action as well as claim, simultaneously maintained three actions against the defendant No. 2; when the defendant No.2 informed the Bombay High Court about the filing of the above Money Suit No. 21 of 1993, Admiralty Suit No. 44 of 1993 and Admiralty Suit No. 20 of 1996 in Bangladesh for the same cause of action and claim Bombay High Court Was about to dismiss the Admiralty Suit No. 44 of 1994 pending before it and also to release the bank guarantee unless the plaintiff withdrew the suits in Bangladesh within 6-11-96; then the plaintiff at first moved an application before the High Court Division for withdrawal of Admiralty Suit No. 20 of 1996 and vide order dated 6-11-96 the High Court Division allowed the same and thereafter the plaintiff on 10-11-96 filed an application in the above Money Suit No. 21 of 1993 praying for withdrawal of the said suit but without seeking any permission to sue afresh and in the above circumstances, the defendant No. 2 filed a written objection to the said application for withdrawal contending that they along with their written statement have already filed a counter-claim for Taka 4,15,27,204 against the plaintiff on payment of due court fees and so in case of withdrawal of the said money suit the defendant No.2 is required to be transposed as the plaintiff of the counter-claim but the learned Subordinate (now Joint District Judge), after hearing, while allowing the above application of the plaintiff for withdrawal of the Money Suit No. 21 of 1993 rejected the prayer of the defendant No. 2 to proceed with the counter-claim as a cross suit by transposing the defendant No.2 as plaintiff in the cross suit on the ground that Order VIII, rule 6, CPC provides for set off and not counter-claim and, as such, the defendant No. 2, who filed counter- claim, cannot be treated as plaintiff in the cross suit. As against that the defendant No. 2 moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 562 of 1997 and after hearing the High Court Division discharged the Rule holding that the plaintiff being permitted to withdraw the suit there remained nothing for the defendant No.2 to make counter-claim in the said suit and that Order VIII, rule 6, CPC provides for set off and does not entitle the defendant No.2 to be transposed as plaintiff and that in the case of United Shipping Corporation Limited vs WH Bennett and others 36 DLR (AD) 175, the Appellate Division, though discussed the implication of new sub-rule 6A which was added to rule 6 of Order VII, CPC in India, but did not observe that the above amended rule 6A is applicable to Order VII, rule 6, CPC of our country. 

 6. In the case of United Shipping vs WH Bennett and others 36 DLR (AD) 175 which was referred by the High Court Division, the trial Court in a suit in which the plaintiff claimed for a decree of Taka 5,85,841 passed order in entertaining the counterclaim for Taka 18,75,000 as an equitable setoff in the suit challenging which the plaintiff moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction which was summarily rejected and the plaintiff then obtained leave to consider whether in the absence of any express provisions for making counter-claim in the Code of Civil Procedure, which only provides for setoff in Order VIII, rule 6, the prayer for counter- claim made by the defendant- respondents in the plaintiff's suit is entertainable or not. From the side of the plaintiff it was contended before this Division that Order VIII, rule 6, CPC makes no express mention of counterclaim and accordingly, the Court has no power to give judgment for the balance of setoff exceeding plaintiff's claim. From the side of the defendant it was contended that the absence of any express provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure for making counter-claim in the plaintiff's suit makes no difference in this respect and a counterclaim by way of equitable set off is entertain able and though the order "counter-claim" finds no reference in Order VIII, rule 6, CPC but in terms of Order XX, rule 19, CPC having provided that "where the defendant has been allowed set off against the claim of the plaintiff, the decree shall state what amount is due to the plaintiff and what amount is due to the defendant and shall be for the recovery of any sum which appears to be due to either party" a counterclaim by way of equitable set off is permissible particularly in view of the discretion of the Court to allow it or not under the provisions of Order VIII, rule 6, CPC and that in the case of United Liner Agencies of Pakistan vs Ehram Jute Baling 27 DLR (AD) 170 it was merely held that the defendants claim arising out of the same transaction could not be set off as provided in Order VIII, rule 6, CPC because the amount of damage claimed was unliquidated and further in AIR 1964 SC 11 it has been held that the counterclaim may be treated as plaint in cross suit though the provisions regarding the contents of a plaint as contained in the Code of Civil Procedure have not been complied with. This Division, quoting the provision of new rule 6A, which was inserted in Order VIII in India by way of amendment, expressly providing for making counter-claim, held as follows: 

 "Although the word "counter-claim" is not used in our statute and although generally speaking a counter-claim is incompetent under the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure and such a claim by the defendant must be enforced in a separate suit, Order VIII, rule 6 read with Order XX, rule 19 does permit what is in essence a counterclaim of a specific kind, namely where the counterclaim is in respect of an ascertained sum of money exceeding the plaintiff's demand and in that case it is permissible for the Court to pass a decree in favour of the defendant for the excess sum over the plaintiffs demand. Although the word set off only is used in Order VIII, rule 6, and not the word counter-claim also, the claim to the ascertained sum of money which the Code permits the defendant to set up in the plaintiff's action for money may not only be what is strictly termed set off but what is also a counter-claim. If the claim set up by the defendant is in respect of a debt what is less than or equal to the plaintiff's claim in the suit, it is a plea of set off pure and simple, but if it exceeds the plaintiff's claim it is to the extent of the excess a cross claim, for the excess he is to be given a decree against the plaintiff in the same action."
